questions.explanation: A boycott uses a shared refusal to buy to put pressure on sellers.
questions.misconception: Confusing a voluntary refusal to buy with having no goods in stock.

questions.stem: Describe how a group of shoppers could communicate a complaint through their buying choices.
hints: Notice whether the group is choosing to buy or refusing to buy.
questions.explanation: Describe a collective refusal to buy the goods. Explain that the refusal sends a complaint about the prices.
questions.misconception: Confusing a voluntary refusal to buy with having no goods in stock.

criteria.description: Describe a collective refusal to buy the goods.
Explain that the refusal sends a complaint about the prices.

questions.stem: A shop has no cloth left. Another shop has cloth but customers refuse to buy it in protest. Which situation illustrates a boycott and why?
hints: Notice whether the group is choosing to buy or refusing to buy.
questions.explanation: Identify the second shop. The refusal is a choice made to express a grievance.
questions.misconception: Confusing a voluntary refusal to buy with having no goods in stock.

criteria.description: Identify the second shop.
The refusal is a choice made to express a grievance.

questions.stem: Design a three-event poster linking the boycott, the shootings of 28 February and the 1948 riots. Explain the difference between ordering events and claiming one single cause.

indicator.subject: History
indicator.content_standard: B5.5.3.1. Show understanding of the sequence of events leading to the 1948 riots in Ghana
indicator.objective: Examine sources of evidence about what happened during the 1948 riots.

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 recognition, 7 simple use, 5 application and 3 challenge questions.

questions.stem: A class map of Accra has a line in its key marked “path authorised for the ex-servicemen”. What does that line represent?
hints: Read the map key before interpreting the route.
questions.explanation: The line records the route that was approved. Other records would be needed to confirm the path taken.
questions.misconception: Assuming that approving a route proves exactly where everyone went.

questions.stem: Which city is named in the exercise on mapping the approved routes for ex-servicemen?
hints: Read the map key before interpreting the route.
questions.explanation: The suggested map is of Accra and shows routes approved for the ex-servicemen.
questions.misconception: Assuming that approving a route proves exactly where everyone went.

questions.stem: Tell a visitor what an approved-route map can show about the ex-servicemen and what it leaves to investigate.
hints: Read the map key before interpreting the route.
questions.explanation: Explain that the map shows a route approved in Accra. Distinguish that approval from proof of the path taken.
questions.misconception: Assuming that approving a route proves exactly where everyone went.

criteria.description: Explain that the map shows a route approved in Accra.
Distinguish that approval from proof of the path taken.

questions.stem: An approved route is drawn on a map. Explain the difference between a route people were allowed to take and the route they actually took.
hints: Read the map key before interpreting the route.
questions.explanation: The map can show what was approved. An account of the march is needed to check the path actually followed.
questions.misconception: Assuming that approving a route proves exactly where everyone went.

criteria.description: The map can show what was approved.
An account of the march is needed to check the path actually followed.

questions.stem: Create a key for a sketch of the march that keeps approved and reported routes distinct. Explain what evidence you need for each.
hints: Read the map key before interpreting the route.
questions.explanation: Use separate symbols with a key. Consult a record of approval for one route and accounts of the day for the other.
questions.misconception: Assuming that approving a route proves exactly where everyone went.

criteria.description: Use separate symbols with a key.
Consult a record of approval for one route and accounts of the day for the other.

questions.stem: In which month were the shootings linked to the 1948 disturbances?

questions.stem: Sketch a simple sequence linking the boycott, the shootings and the riots, giving the February date to the right event.

questions.explanation: Show the boycott, shootings and riots as linked events. Attach 28 February to the shootings.

hints: Ask whose arrest is described.
questions.explanation: The enquiry links the Big Six, leaders associated with the UGCC, with their arrest. The arrest is distinct from the shooting of ex-servicemen.

questions.stem: What collective name was given to the six UGCC leaders whose arrests are studied with the disturbances?

questions.stem: Add a label to a timeline that identifies the group of leaders arrested in connection with the disturbances.

questions.misconception: Confusing the leaders arrested with the ex-servicemen who were shot.

criteria.description: The first concerns what happened to ex-servicemen.

criteria.description: Arrest records what authorities did to the leaders.
A claim about responsibility needs separate evidence about actions.

hints: Check how the filmmaker distinguishes a source from a reconstruction.
questions.explanation: A documentary can combine source material and later interpretation to present a historical event.

questions.stem: Write one question to ask about a documentary's evidence and one question about a claim it makes about the riots.
hints: Check how the filmmaker distinguishes a source from a reconstruction.
questions.explanation: Ask where a particular image or account came from. Ask how it supports the documentary's account of what happened.

Ask how it supports the documentary's account of what happened.

questions.stem: In a film about the riots a narrator speaks over an old image. Explain why you would examine the image and the commentary separately.
hints: Check how the filmmaker distinguishes a source from a reconstruction.
questions.explanation: The image may give visual evidence tied to a date and place. The later commentary interprets what the viewer sees.
questions.misconception: Treating every scene in a later production as original footage.

criteria.description: The image may give visual evidence tied to a date and place.
The later commentary interprets what the viewer sees.
